scenes.visual: Title card 'The Price of a Breath' fades in over a pale green barley field seen from the side, 16:9. COLOUR MAP, same in every scene and in the second film: carbon dioxide = TEAL arrows; water vapour = BLUE arrows; oxygen = WARM RED arrows; guard cells and stomata = PURPLE; 'the price' (water lost per gas gained) = a GOLD balance scale; waxy layer, cells and labels = GREY. Leaf A = solid outline, leaf B = dashed outline. Cartoon schematics only, no molecular structures; every bar or gauge not computed is labelled 'schematic'. Numbers appear only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: Why can't a leaf take carbon dioxide from the air without losing water? Taking something in often carries a cost somewhere else. A leaf makes that cost easy to see.
scenes.visual: A single cartoon barley leaf sways. Thin TEAL arrows drift toward it from the air; at the same moment BLUE arrows stream away from it. Question card: 'Why can't a leaf take carbon dioxide without losing water?'
scenes.narration: Why can't a leaf take carbon dioxide from the air without losing water? Taking something in often carries a cost somewhere else. A leaf makes that cost easy to see.

scenes.tts: Every multicellular organism faces the same five problems. Get energy and materials. Exchange and move them, wastes included. Keep its inside relatively stable. Resist damage and invasion. Leave descendants.
scenes.visual: A five-row checklist builds on the left, one row per spoken item: 'energy and materials', 'exchange and transport (wastes too)', 'a stable inside', 'defense', 'reproduction'. Each row ticks as it is named. Three small cartoon icons on the right: barley plant, honeybee, human.
scenes.narration: Every multicellular organism faces the same five problems. Get energy and materials. Exchange and move them, wastes included. Keep its inside relatively stable. Resist damage and invasion. Leave descendants.

scenes.tts: Barley, honeybee or human, each body solves all five. Many solutions carry a cost, paid somewhere else. The exchange problem shows that cost most clearly.
scenes.visual: Ticks appear beside each icon for every row. A GOLD price tag with a question mark swings onto each row. The row 'exchange and transport' glows and its tag fills in; the camera dives toward the barley leaf's surface.
scenes.narration: Barley, honeybee or human, each body solves all five. Many solutions carry a cost, paid somewhere else. The exchange problem shows that cost most clearly.

scenes.tts: Zoom into a barley leaf. A waxy layer covers the surface, and water crosses it poorly. So gas moves mainly through pores called stomata. Two guard cells flank each pore and open or close the gap.
scenes.visual: Cross-section cartoon of a leaf: a GREY waxy band along the top surface, beads of water bouncing off it. A gap in the band flanked by two bean-shaped PURPLE guard cells, labelled 'stoma (pore)' and 'guard cells'. The guard cells swell apart and the gap widens.
scenes.narration: Zoom into a barley leaf. A waxy layer covers the surface, and water crosses it poorly. So gas moves mainly through pores called stomata. Two guard cells flank each pore and open or close the gap.

scenes.tts: Inside the leaf, cell walls line air spaces, and those walls are wet. Carbon dioxide must dissolve in that water film to reach the cells. But a wet surface open to air loses water.
scenes.visual: Camera passes through the pore into an air space ringed by GREY cells with a glistening wet film on their walls, labelled 'wet cell walls'. TEAL arrows enter through the pore and sink into the film. BLUE wisps rise off the film.
scenes.narration: Inside the leaf, cell walls line air spaces, and those walls are wet. Carbon dioxide must dissolve in that water film to reach the cells. But a wet surface open to air loses water.

scenes.tts: So water vapour leaves through the same pore that lets carbon dioxide in. Both gases take one path. What, then, sets the price, the water lost for each carbon gained?
scenes.visual: Side by side at the pore: a few thin TEAL arrows going in, many thick BLUE arrows going out through the same gap. A GOLD balance scale appears beside the pore, labelled 'the price = water lost / carbon gained'.
scenes.narration: So water vapour leaves through the same pore that lets carbon dioxide in. Both gases take one path. What, then, sets the price, the water lost for each carbon gained?

scenes.tts: Look at two gaps across the pore. First, the carbon dioxide gap. Carbon dioxide is a tiny share of air, and the leaf draws it down only part of the way.
scenes.visual: Two gauges rise beside the pore, labelled 'inside' and 'outside'. A TEAL bar labelled 'CO2 gap' grows to only a short height. On-screen text: 'CO2 ≈ 0.04% of air'. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Look at two gaps across the pore. First, the carbon dioxide gap. Carbon dioxide is a tiny share of air, and the leaf draws it down only part of the way.

scenes.tts: Now the water gap. Air inside a leaf is saturated with water vapour, while outside air is drier. That gap is far bigger. So the leaf pays hundreds of water molecules for each carbon dioxide.
scenes.visual: A BLUE bar labelled 'water gap' shoots up beside the short TEAL bar, about a hundred times taller; the camera tilts up to follow it. On-screen text: 'water gap ≈ 100 × CO2 gap (moderately dry air)'. The GOLD scale tips hard: one TEAL dot on one pan, a heap of BLUE dots on the other, labelled 'hundreds of H2O per CO2 (depends on the air)'.
scenes.narration: Now the water gap. Air inside a leaf is saturated with water vapour, while outside air is drier. That gap is far bigger. So the leaf pays hundreds of water molecules for each carbon dioxide.

scenes.tts: Now let the guard cells narrow the pore, with both gaps held fixed. Both streams shrink together. The pores set how fast gas moves. The two gaps set the price.
scenes.visual: The PURPLE guard cells sag toward each other and the gap narrows. TEAL and BLUE arrow streams both thin by the same proportion. The GOLD scale stays tipped at the same angle. On-screen text: 'gaps held fixed for now' and 'pores → how fast; gaps → the price'.
scenes.narration: Now let the guard cells narrow the pore, with both gaps held fixed. Both streams shrink together. The pores set how fast gas moves. The two gaps set the price.

scenes.tts: Your lung also moves a gas across a wet surface. It takes in oxygen. Will it pay more water for each molecule of gas, or less?
scenes.visual: Cut to a cartoon human chest; inside, a cluster of tiny moist air sacs glistens. WARM RED arrows enter with each breath; BLUE wisps leave on the breath out. Question card: 'More water per molecule, or less?'
scenes.narration: Your lung also moves a gas across a wet surface. It takes in oxygen. Will it pay more water for each molecule of gas, or less?

scenes.visual: Question card holds. The chest rises and falls slowly; a small timer ring fills.

scenes.tts: Far less. Oxygen is plentiful in air, so each breath can hand over a lot of it. The breath out carries away about as much water vapour. So the lung pays about one water molecule for each oxygen.
scenes.visual: Beside the lung, a breath balance: an 'air in' column and an 'air out' column. The WARM RED oxygen band drops from 'about 21%' in to 'about 16%' out; the BLUE water band rises from 'about 1%' in to 'about 5 to 6%' out. A second GOLD scale nearly balances: one RED dot against about one BLUE dot. On-screen text: 'about 1 H2O per O2 (varies with breathing, temperature and humidity)'. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Far less. Oxygen is plentiful in air, so each breath can hand over a lot of it. The breath out carries away about as much water vapour. So the lung pays about one water molecule for each oxygen.

scenes.tts: But the lung cannot close the way a stoma can. It sits sheltered deep in the chest. In ordinary unsaturated air, narrowing or sheltering a path can cut the water cost. But while gas keeps flowing in, some water still leaves.
scenes.visual: Split screen: on the left the PURPLE guard cells nearly close the leaf pore and both arrow streams shrink to a trickle, with one faint BLUE wisp still leaving through the waxy layer, labelled 'nearly closed'; on the right the lung keeps breathing inside the GREY rib cage, BLUE wisps still leaving. Text: 'only the leaf can close' and 'unsaturated air'. The two GOLD scales sit side by side, neither empty.
scenes.narration: But the lung cannot close the way a stoma can. It sits sheltered deep in the chest. In ordinary unsaturated air, narrowing or sheltering a path can cut the water cost. But while gas keeps flowing in, some water still leaves.

scenes.tts: Back to the checklist. For every row, ask what a solution costs, and where that cost is paid. Then ask how you would test it.
scenes.visual: The five-row checklist returns with barley, honeybee and human icons. A GOLD price tag with a question mark hangs on every row; the 'exchange' tag is filled in and shows the tiny leaf-and-lung scales.
scenes.narration: Back to the checklist. For every row, ask what a solution costs, and where that cost is paid. Then ask how you would test it.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'In unsaturated air, a leaf pays water for carbon; gaps set the price.'
